claims.text: The initial titanium–nickel-based HEA is a single-phase solid solution with no secondary phases.
The proposed intervention is solutionizing at 1100–1200°C followed by aging at approximately 600°C for 2 hours under argon.
Solutionizing at 1100–1200°C will ensure compositional homogeneity.
Aging at approximately 600°C for 2 hours will produce nanoscale intermetallic precipitates.
The precipitates will be fine and uniformly dispersed within the matrix.
The precipitated phase may be Ni3Ti or another Ti-rich intermetallic phase.
Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion produces precipitation strengthening.
Precipitation strengthening will increase high-temperature yield strength.
The precipitates will reduce creep deformation and creep rate.
The aged alloy will show a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to the as-cast, unaged alloy at 500–700°C.
The aged alloy will show a statistically significant improvement in creep resistance relative to the as-cast, unaged alloy at 500–700°C.
The intervention is applicable to HEAs in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
The intervention remains effective only if nanoscale precipitates form without compromising the alloy's overall single-phase integrity.

contradictions.description: The intervention is explicitly intended to create an intermetallic precipitate phase, which makes the material multiphase, while the boundary requires preservation of overall single-phase integrity. This could be coherent only if 'single-phase' refers narrowly to the matrix, but the hypothesis does not make that distinction consistently.
